units: a short cooking time is needed to obtain a firm bite
too much sauce softens a firm preparation
gentle, lengthy heat loosens the fibres without drying them out
patient sieving gives a smooth preparation that coats the palate
a smooth texture takes the edge off harsh flavours
liquid poured in cold causes lumps in a purée
flesh full of fibres signals a badly chosen cut
an over-wet batter gives a cake that sinks like a sponge
texture is judged before taste
text: Three textures rule the plate of a careful cook, and each answers to rules of its own. Crispness comes first. It demands a brief cooking time, firm ingredients and a restrained dressing, since a generous sauce softens it at once. Meltingness takes second place, born of low heat held over a long stretch, which loosens the fibres without drying them out. Smoothness closes the set: won by patient sieving, it coats the palate and rounds off flavours that would otherwise cut too sharply. Alongside these three families sit the mishaps every cook dreads. A lumpy purée gives away liquid poured in straight from the cold. Stringy meat announces a badly chosen cut. A spongy cake reveals a batter swollen with damp. Knowing these faults counts for as much as mastering the successes, because texture is judged before flavour ever comes into it.

units: talk about cooking has shifted as households cooked less
speed was praised first
industry claimed to set free whoever prepared the meals
ready-made dishes were then taken to task for tasting of nothing
they were blamed for carrying too much salt
cooking programmes put the working hand on show
home kitchens never followed that display
a newer line of argument weighs a plate by its price and its origin
each phase corrected what the one before had overdone
text: The way people talk about cooking has shifted, and it shifted as households cooked less and less. Speed came first: a meal had to fit into a narrow gap in the day, and industry pledged to set free whoever stood at the stove. The mood then turned. Ready-made dishes were taken to task for tasting of nothing much at all, and the salt they carried was called excessive. Cooking programmes answered by putting the working hand on show, though what went on in home kitchens never really followed the display. A newer line of argument now weighs a plate by its price and by where its contents came from. None of this sequence is absurd: each stage corrected what the one before had overdone. It leaves a question nobody has settled, all the same. Who still has the room to cook without pressure bearing down on them?

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the baker puts her skill down to a childhood spent beside the family mill
she turned down ready-mixed flours
that refusal cost her custom at the start
her dough rises at its own pace
the slow rise thickens the crust
her bread gives off a faintly sharp smell that throws new customers
many disappointed customers come back because the bread keeps for a week
her bake is gone before the middle of the day
she puts her success down to stubbornness rather than a gift
text: Ask the baker down the road where that dense loaf of hers comes from, and she will tell you she can hardly take the credit for it. Her parents ran a mill, so she grew up with her hands in the flour, and the habit settled everything that came after. Because she could tell the grains apart by touch from an early age, she turned down the ready-mixed flours, and the choice cost her custom at the start. Her dough rises at its own pace, so the crust thickens and the faintly sharp smell throws newcomers. Plenty of people leave disappointed, then come back again, because a loaf like that keeps for a whole week. She has never needed a sign above the shop: the bake is gone before midday and the queue spills out onto the pavement. Stubbornness, she says with a laugh, is what did it, not a gift.

units: this establishment listed more dishes than its kitchen could handle
the broth came through with no flavour at the first service
a heavy sauce flattened a delicate fish
the chocolate pudding felt rough under the spoon
the front of house did its job properly
the manager cut the menu in half
a cook brought in from a country inn took over the slow cooking
plates went out hotter and the wait shortened within the week
a short menu is presented here as the condition of decent cooking
text: The place that has just opened at the far end of the busy shopping street was suffering from a common complaint: a menu far too long, listing dishes that its own kitchen could not handle. The first service made that plain enough. The broth came through with no flavour at all, a heavy sauce flattened a delicate fish, and the chocolate pudding felt rough under the spoon. The front of house, in fairness, did its job well. The manager took the knife to the menu and cut it in half, then handed the slow cooking over to a cook brought in from a country inn. The difference showed within the week: plates went out hotter, the wait shortened, and the evening service coped without extra hands. A short menu is no confession of poverty. Here it is the very condition of decent cooking.

units: the woman written to describes her new kitchen as nothing like the old one
the old kitchen smelt of damp wood and baked fruit
the new one gives off a smell of metal and soap
the copper pan heated unevenly
the sauce had to be watched the whole time
the newer hob answers the dial at once
the writer reads this as a trade rather than an improvement
the old soups had a cloudy colour and a strong flavour
vegetables cooked in the new kitchen keep some firmness
text: You write that the kitchen you cook in now bears no likeness to the one we once shared, and I think I follow you. Ours smelt of damp wood and baked pear; yours, you say, smells of metal and of soap. With us the copper pan heated unevenly, and a sauce had to be watched the way one watches a child. With you the hob answers the dial at once and nothing boils over. I read that as a trade rather than an improvement. You have gained precision and you have lost the waiting. Our soups took on a cloudy colour and a deep flavour that your bright kitchen will never draw out; yours, on the other hand, leave the vegetables a firmness we knew nothing about. Write and tell me what you make in the evenings. I should like to picture the steam on your windows as I still see it rising from ours.

units: the hold of an emulsion rests on three separate things
an egg yolk or mustard wraps the droplets of fat
that coating keeps the droplets from running together
oil trickled in slowly gives the binder time to work
a sudden pour of oil breaks the mixture
very cold liquid sets part of the fat and leaves lumps
a split sauce is rescued by starting again from a fresh yolk in a clean bowl
the failed mixture is worked back in a little at a time
an emulsion that has held looks almost clear at the edges
text: What separates a stable emulsion from one that has split? Its hold rests on three things, and each of them can be looked at on its own. The first is the binder: an egg yolk, or a touch of mustard, wraps the droplets of fat and keeps them from running together. The second is the pace of the mixing. Oil trickled in slowly gives the binder the time to do its work, whereas a sudden pour breaks the whole thing at once. The third is temperature: liquid straight from the cold sets part of the fat and leaves a lumpy mass behind. And how is a split sauce rescued? Start again from a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then work the failed mixture back into it a little at a time, without hurrying. An emulsion that has held together looks almost clear at the edges and velvety at the centre.

units: the head waiter tells the junior cook that every table will be taken
the junior cook says he prepared the garnishes as soon as the doors opened
only the herbs are missing
the buyer reports that the delivery will arrive late
she suggests using a spiced relish kept in a jar
the head waiter agrees on condition that the menu says so
a guest finds his dish too salty in the middle of service
the junior cook accepts the mistake and offers to make the plate again
not a single order was lost in the end
text: At the start of service the head waiter reminded the junior cook that every table would be taken. The junior cook replied that he had prepared the garnishes as soon as the doors opened, and that only the herbs were missing. The buyer then announced that the delivery would arrive late, and she suggested a spiced relish kept in a jar in place of fresh leaves. The head waiter hesitated before agreeing, on condition that the menu said so. Around the middle of service a guest remarked that his dish tasted too salty; the junior cook owned the mistake and offered a fresh plate at once, which the room carried out with no noticeable delay. At the close of the evening the buyer summed matters up before the assembled staff: not a single order had been lost, and everyone had been equal to the work.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food once rested on salt, smoke and sugar
these constraints shaped tastes that lasted
salt drew the water out of flesh, so it had to be soaked out before cooking
root vegetables were added to broths to balance a flavour that came through too strong
smoke left sharp compounds on the surface of the joints
cooks rubbed those joints with herbs and fat to soften the attack
sugar was kept for fruit because it was scarcer
mechanical cold made these methods unnecessary
the methods lived on as tastes people look for
text: Long before mechanical cold reached the kitchen, keeping food rested on salt, on smoke and on sugar alone. That constraint went on to shape whole tastes. Because salt drew the water out of flesh, it had to be soaked out again before cooking, and broths filled up with root vegetables to balance a flavour that came through far too strong. Because smoke left sharp compounds on the surface of a joint, cooks learnt to rub the outside with herbs and fat and soften the attack. Sugar, being scarcer, went to fruit, whose flesh it turned clear and yielding. When the ice box and then the cooling machine spread, none of these methods was needed any more, yet none of them died out either. They had become tastes that people look for, and they now cost a good deal more than something fresh.

units: sticky rice turns into a pasty lump as it cooks
the pan is rarely the main cause
the grain gives off starch the moment it heats in water
that starch behaves like glue
rinsing the grain until the water runs clear solves part of the problem
measuring the water avoids a longer cooking time
a longer cooking time crushes the grains
cutting the heat before the end lets the steam finish the job
salting the water at the start puts right a flavour that is too faint
text: Rice sticking together in a pasty lump? It happens far more often than you would think, and the pan is rarely the one to blame. The grain gives off its starch the moment it heats in water, and that starch behaves like glue. First thing to do: rinse the rice under cold water until what runs off it is clear, then leave it to drain. Second: measure the water instead of splashing it in, because too much of it means a longer cooking time, and a longer cooking time crushes the grains. Third: cut the heat before the stated end, put the lid on tight and let the steam finish the job without stirring. If it still tastes flat to you, salt the water at the start rather than the plate at the end. You will get separate grains, firm to the bite, that will take any sauce without falling apart.

units: a broken oven turned a caterer's evening upside down
the team shifted the whole menu onto fierce direct heat
the guests compared two ways of cooking without meaning to
root vegetables roasted the day before had a soft centre and a sweet surface
the same vegetables seared in the pan held a marked firmness and a plain bitterness
fish cooked in the oven had soft, airy flesh
fish cooked over the flame had brittle skin and denser flesh
the guests who were asked split into two camps of much the same size
the caterer now offers both ways of cooking
text: A broken oven turned a caterer's evening into an experiment that nobody had planned for. With no dry heat left to work with, the team shifted the whole menu onto fierce direct flame, and the guests found themselves comparing two ways of cooking without meaning to. The day before, the same root vegetables had roasted slowly: soft at the centre, sweet on the surface, rounded in smell. That night, seared in the pan, they held a marked firmness and a plain bitterness closer to the raw plant. The fish went the same way. From the oven it gave soft, airy flesh; over the flame the skin turned brittle and the inside came out denser. Asked on the way out, the guests split into two camps of much the same size. The caterer took the point and now offers both, letting the room decide.
